sandhi.note: Visarga before t becomes s; the t of तत् becomes c next to c (तच्च); च + ऐक्यम्: a + ai → ai. The final m becomes anusvāra before s (मोऽनुस्वारः, 8.3.23).

samasa.literal: those of whom Śakra is the first
samasa.sense: Indra and all the other gods

samasa.type: tatpuruṣa with the prefix सु (prādi type)

morph.note: Imperfect of सम् + √गम् with augment a- (सम्-अ-गच्छ-त). With सम्, √गम् takes ātmanepada endings in the sense ‘to come together’. ऐक्यं समगच्छत: ‘went into oneness’, i.e. merged.
The taddhita -तः (तसिल्) gives an ablative sense: ‘from the body’. The singular is distributive: from the body of each god.

mantras.anvaya: अन्येषां च एव शक्रादीनां देवानां शरीरतः सुमहत् तेजः निर्गतम्। तत् च ऐक्यं समगच्छत।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: the tejas came out (निर्गतम्, participle as verb), and it merged (समगच्छत).
mantras.lit: And from the bodies of the other gods too, Śakra and the rest, came out a very great radiance; and that came together into oneness.
mantras.tr: From the bodies of the other gods as well, Indra and the rest, a great radiance poured forth, and all of it came together and became one.

comm.t: After the three great gods, all the others give their tejas, and it all merges. The Goddess will not be the tejas of any one god but of all of them together.

The gods’ hymn in chapter 4 says this outright: the Goddess’s form is the gathered power of all the hosts of gods (4.3, निश्शेषदेवगणशक्तिसमूहमूर्त्या). The tradition reads this as the unity of the divine powers, which the gods could not achieve as separate beings but she embodies.

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi containing a tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa (ज्वालाव्याप्त) and a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (दिगन्तर)
samasa.literal: that by which the space of the quarters is pervaded with flames
samasa.sense: filling every direction with its flames
samasa.alt: Grammatically it could also qualify पर्वतम् (m. acc. sg. has the same ending); it is the mass of tejas, not the mountain of the simile, that the gods see filling the quarters.

morph.note: Present participle of √ज्वल्, accusative singular masculine, agreeing with पर्वतम्: ‘a mountain on fire’.
Perfect of √दृश् (reduplicated द-दृश्), third person plural: ‘they saw’.

mantras.anvaya: ते सुराः तत्र ज्वलन्तं पर्वतम् इव अतीव तेजसः कूटं ज्वालाव्याप्तदिगन्तरं ददृशुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject (ते सुराः), verb (ददृशुः), and an object (तेजसः कूटम्) with a simile and a bahuvrīhi describing it.
mantras.lit: Those gods saw there an immense mass of radiance, like a blazing mountain, whose flames filled the space of the quarters.
mantras.tr: There the gods saw a vast mass of light like a mountain on fire, its flames filling every direction.

comm.t: Before it takes a form, the merged tejas is seen as a burning mountain that fills space. The gods are spectators of what they have given.
A modern reading: what the gods could not do apart becomes visible when their powers are pooled. The image is of overwhelming, undirected force, waiting for a form.

samasa.sense: drawn from every god at once

samasa.literal: that by which the triad of worlds is pervaded

morph.note: Neuter, so it qualifies तत् तेजः, not नारी (a feminine would be व्याप्तलोकत्रया, as the Goddess herself is called in 2.37, व्याप्तलोकत्रयां त्विषा). The radiance that already filled the three worlds became a woman.
Aorist of √भू with a predicate nominative: तत् … नारी अभूत्, ‘it became a woman’. The neuter subject and the feminine predicate stand side by side: the transformation is in the grammar.

mantras.anvaya: तत्र सर्वदेवशरीरजम् अतुलं तत् तेजः एकस्थं (सत्), त्विषा व्याप्तलोकत्रयं तत् नारी अभूत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A neuter subject (तत् तेजः, resumed by the second तत्) with its qualifiers, a feminine predicate (नारी) and the verb अभूत्.
mantras.lit: There that matchless radiance, born from the bodies of all the gods, gathered into one, which had pervaded the three worlds with its brilliance, became a woman.
mantras.tr: There that matchless radiance, born from the bodies of all the gods, gathered into one place and, filling the three worlds with its light, became a woman.
mantras.tr_note: tr keeps व्याप्तलोकत्रयम् with the radiance, as the neuter requires, but turns it into a participial phrase.

comm.t: The central moment of the chapter: the combined tejas becomes a woman. The verse is carefully neuter until the last noun: it is the radiance (तेजः, n.) that is matchless, gathered and world-filling, and that radiance ‘became a woman’ (नारी अभूत्).

Medhas has already said that the Goddess is eternal and is called ‘born’ only when she becomes manifest for the gods’ purpose (1.64–66: देवानां कार्यसिद्ध्यर्थमाविर्भवति सा यदा). The tradition therefore reads this verse as a manifestation, not a creation: the gods’ tejas gives her a visible form; it does not bring her into being.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) opens with a similar emergence: name 4, चिदग्निकुण्डसम्भूता, ‘she who arose from the fire-pit of consciousness’, and name 5, देवकार्यसमुद्यता, ‘she who is intent on the gods’ purpose’. There she rises from a sacrificial fire, here from the gods’ combined tejas; the two accounts are distinct.

samasa.sense: the woman’s face; inside the compound the pronoun appears as तद् whatever its gender, and t becomes n before m (यरोऽनुनासिकेऽनुनासिको वा, 8.4.45)
samasa.alt: It could also be read as two words, तत् मुखम् ‘that face’; the compound reading matches तदङ्गुल्यः in 2.16, where the pronoun cannot agree with its noun and must be a compound member.

samasa.sense: from Viṣṇu’s share of the tejas

morph.note: Imperfect of √जन् (stem जाय-, divādi, ātmanepada): ‘was born’. The parts of the body are ‘born’ from each god’s tejas.
Taddhita of relation with vṛddhi of the first vowel: शम्भु → शाम्भव ‘of Śambhu’. याम्य (from यम) is formed the same way with -य; both stand for ‘the tejas of …’.

mantras.anvaya: यत् शाम्भवं तेजः अभूत्, तेन तन्मुखम् अजायत। याम्येन (तेजसा) च केशाः अभवन्, विष्णुतेजसा बाहवः (अभवन्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (यत् … अभूत्) answered by तेन; then two short clauses with the instrumental of the source.
mantras.lit: The radiance that was Śambhu’s — by that her face was formed; and by Yama’s the hair came to be; the arms by the radiance of Viṣṇu.
mantras.tr: From Śiva’s radiance her face was formed; from Yama’s, her hair; from Viṣṇu’s, her arms.
mantras.tr_note: tr compresses the relative construction (यत् … तेन) into a simple ‘from’.

comm.t: The second movement begins: each god’s tejas forms one part of the woman’s body (2.14–18). Śiva gives the face, Yama the hair, Viṣṇu the arms.

A modern reading: the pairings invite reflection (the arms that will hold the weapons from Viṣṇu the preserver, the dark hair from Yama, lord of death), but the text itself states only the correspondence and gives no reasons.

samasa.sense: the legs, below and above the knee; the compound takes the gender of its last member (ऊरु, m.)
samasa.alt: Names of body parts are usually joined in a samāhāra dvandva (neuter singular, जङ्घोरु); the text has the dual जङ्घोरू, an itaretara dvandva counting the two kinds of limb.

morph.note: Nominative dual of the itaretara dvandva: two members, so dual, although each limb is itself a pair. Epic usage; the classical rule would prefer the neuter collective.
Imperfect singular of √भू. It agrees with the nearest subject (मध्यम्), and is understood with the other subjects of the verse.
Genitive singular of the feminine root-noun भू ‘Earth’ (ū → uv before vowel endings): the Earth as a goddess giving her tejas.

mantras.anvaya: सौम्येन (तेजसा) स्तनयोः युग्मम् (अभवत्), ऐन्द्रेण च मध्यम् अभवत्, वारुणेन च जङ्घोरू (अभवताम्), भुवः तेजसा नितम्बः (अभवत्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Four parallel clauses, each with the source in the instrumental and the body part as subject; अभवत् is stated once and understood in the rest.
mantras.lit: By Soma’s (radiance) the pair of breasts, and by Indra’s the waist came to be; and by Varuṇa’s the shanks and thighs; the hips by the radiance of the Earth.
mantras.tr: From the Moon’s radiance her breasts were formed, from Indra’s her waist, from Varuṇa’s her legs, and from the Earth’s radiance her hips.

comm.t: The forming of the body continues: breasts from Soma, waist from Indra, legs from Varuṇa, hips from the Earth. The givers include the Earth, a goddess, alongside the gods.

The Purāṇa describes the Goddess’s body plainly, part by part, and the passage is recited as it stands. Its point is that no part of her is the gift of a single deity: she is assembled from the whole pantheon, the Earth included.
